title: Solar System: Habitability Within and Beyond
summary: What would it take for a place to be habitable, how would we know from here, and which worlds actually qualify? Work from the physics of light and gravity to the evidence returned by specific spacecraft.
objectives: State the conditions a world must meet to be habitable, and apply them to a named object.
Compute equilibrium temperature, flux, escape velocity and orbital quantities without a calculator.
Read the evidence for subsurface oceans, past surface water and atmospheric composition, and say which instrument produced it.
Describe how each exoplanet detection method works and what it can and cannot measure.
Explain how water and organic material are delivered, and what the building blocks of life are.
Match a mission to its science objective, its instruments and the trade-offs behind its design.

units.title: What Makes a World Habitable
units.summary: Habitability is a set of conditions, not a verdict; naming them is what makes the rest of the event answerable.
objectives: Name the conditions for habitability and the energy, solvent and chemistry each requires.
Define the habitable zone and say why its edges move with the star.

lessons.title: Energy, Solvent, Chemistry
lessons.objective: State what a habitable environment requires — an energy source, a stable liquid solvent, and the elements life is built from — and apply the list to a named world.

lessons.title: The Habitable Zone and Equilibrium Temperature
lessons.objective: Define the circumstellar habitable zone, and compute an equilibrium temperature from stellar flux and albedo.

lessons.title: Keeping an Atmosphere
lessons.objective: Explain how escape velocity, temperature and molecular mass decide which gases a world retains, and describe the escape processes that strip an atmosphere.

units.title: Reading Worlds by Their Light
units.summary: Almost everything known about a distant world arrives as light; the laws that govern it are examinable arithmetic.
objectives: Apply the Stefan-Boltzmann law, Wien's law and the inverse-square law to real quantities.
Explain how a spectrum identifies surface and atmospheric composition.

lessons.title: Flux, Blackbodies, Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien
lessons.objective: Use the Stefan-Boltzmann law and Wien's displacement law, and scale flux with the inverse-square law.

lessons.title: Spectra: What a World Is Made Of
lessons.objective: Distinguish emission from absorption spectra and explain how transmission spectroscopy reads an exoplanet atmosphere.

lessons.title: Doppler Shift and Motion
lessons.objective: Relate a wavelength shift to motion along the line of sight, and say what that measures for a star with a planet.

units.title: Gravity, Orbits and Tides
units.summary: Orbits set the temperature, and tides supply the heat where sunlight cannot reach.
objectives: Apply Newton's law of gravitation and Kepler's three laws.
Explain tidal forces and how tidal heating powers an ocean world.

lessons.title: Newton, Kepler and Orbital Arithmetic
lessons.objective: Apply Newton's law of universal gravitation and Kepler's three laws, including the period-semimajor axis relation.

lessons.title: Tidal Forces and Tidal Heating
lessons.objective: Explain tidal force as differential gravity, and how orbital eccentricity and resonance convert it into internal heat.

lessons.title: Kinetic and Potential Energy in Orbit
lessons.objective: Track kinetic and gravitational potential energy around an eccentric orbit and in tidal flexing.

units.title: Water, Ice and the Building Blocks
units.summary: The solvent and the chemistry: what forms water takes off Earth, and what life is assembled from.
objectives: Distinguish liquid water, crystalline and amorphous ice, brines and clathrates, and where each occurs.
Name the four classes of biological building block and the chemistry behind them.

lessons.title: Liquid, Ice, Brine and Clathrate
lessons.objective: Describe the phases and forms water takes across the Solar System, including amorphous ice, brines and clathrate hydrates, and the conditions each requires.

lessons.title: Proteins, Nucleic Acids, Lipids, Carbohydrates
lessons.objective: Name the four classes of biological macromolecule and the elements they require, and say what each one tells a mission looking for habitable conditions or biosignatures.

lessons.title: Extremophiles and the Limits of Life
lessons.objective: Describe chemolithoautotrophic metabolism and tardigrade survival, and use terrestrial extremes as analogs for habitable environments off Earth.

units.title: How Water and Organics Get Delivered
units.summary: Small bodies carry the volatiles; their isotopes record where the water came from.
objectives: Explain cometary and asteroidal delivery of water and organics and the isotopic evidence for each.
Describe what sample return from Bennu and Rosetta's visit to 67P actually found.

lessons.title: Comets, Asteroids and the Kuiper Belt
lessons.objective: Describe comet and asteroid composition and structure, and where the Solar System stores its volatiles.

lessons.title: Where Earth's Water Came From
lessons.objective: Use the D/H ratio to argue for cometary versus asteroidal delivery, and cite what Bennu and 67P samples contained.

units.title: Venus and Mars: Two Failed Experiments
units.summary: Two neighbours that started habitable-looking and ended otherwise; the difference is the lesson.
objectives: Explain the runaway greenhouse on Venus and the loss of the Martian atmosphere.
Read the morphological evidence for past liquid water on Mars.

lessons.title: Venus: A Runaway Greenhouse
lessons.objective: Describe Venus's atmosphere, surface conditions and water loss, and explain the runaway greenhouse that produced them.

lessons.title: Mars: Reading a Wetter Past
lessons.objective: Identify the morphological and mineralogical evidence for past liquid water on Mars, and describe present-day brines and ice.

lessons.title: Where the Martian Atmosphere Went
lessons.objective: Explain how the loss of a global magnetic field and low gravity allowed solar wind stripping, and what MAVEN measured.

units.title: Ocean Worlds
units.summary: The best candidates for life today are moons with oceans under ice, and the evidence for those oceans is indirect and clever.
objectives: Cite the evidence for a subsurface ocean at Europa, Enceladus, Ganymede and Titan.
Explain cryovolcanism and what plume chemistry reveals.

lessons.title: Europa and Ganymede
lessons.objective: Describe Europa's ice shell and chaos terrain and Ganymede's interior, and explain how an induced magnetic field reveals a salty ocean.

lessons.title: Enceladus: Sampling an Ocean From Space
lessons.objective: Describe the south-polar plumes and tiger stripes, and what silica grains and organics in the plume imply about hydrothermal activity.

lessons.title: Titan: A Methane Cycle and an Ocean Below
lessons.objective: Describe Titan's atmosphere, methane lakes and haze chemistry, and what Dragonfly is designed to measure.

lessons.title: Makemake and the Distant Ices
lessons.objective: Describe Makemake's properties and surface ices, and why distant dwarf planets are poor habitability candidates.

units.title: Habitability Beyond the Solar System
units.summary: Four detection methods, each measuring something different, and three systems the manual names.
objectives: Explain transit, radial velocity, microlensing and direct imaging, and what each measures.
Describe TRAPPIST-1, Kepler-452 and LHS 1140 and why each is interesting.

lessons.title: Transits and Radial Velocity
lessons.objective: Relate transit depth to planet radius and radial-velocity amplitude to mass, and explain why the two methods together give density.

lessons.title: Microlensing and Direct Imaging
lessons.objective: Explain gravitational microlensing light curves and the contrast problem direct imaging must solve.

lessons.title: TRAPPIST-1, Kepler-452 and LHS 1140
lessons.objective: Describe each named system's star, planets and habitable-zone members, and what JWST has measured there.

units.title: Missions, Instruments and Competition Application
units.summary: Every claim in this event traces to an instrument on a spacecraft; the last step is turning that into points.
objectives: Match mission to objective, instrument and design trade-off.
Work calculator-free and read data displays under time.

lessons.title: What a Mission Is Built To Answer
lessons.objective: For each named mission, state its science objective, its key instruments, and one engineering trade-off its design reflects.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Without a Calculator
lessons.objective: Rearrange a formula symbolically, carry scientific notation, use dimensional analysis as a check, and estimate to an order of magnitude.

lessons.title: Reading Data Under Time
lessons.objective: Given a spectrum, a light curve, an image and a table for one object, build one consistent account of what it says about habitability.
